query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of chromium (Cr) into the refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) WVTaTi will improve its high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: WVTaTi RHEA with varying amounts of Cr
generation.intervention: Addition of Cr to the WVTaTi alloy system
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (up to 900 °C) and mechanical loading
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a BCC solid solution phase and precipitation of Cr-rich phases
generation.mechanism: The addition of Cr promotes the formation of a Laves phase with AB2 stoichiometry, which enhances the high-temperature mechanical properties of the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature mechanical capability, limited density increase, and preserved room-temperature performance
generation.boundary: Temperature range: up to 900 °C, loading conditions: compressive yield strength
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Cr required to achieve the optimal balance of properties is uncertain and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare WVTaTi RHEA samples with varying amounts of Cr (0, 5, 10 at.%) and test their high-temperature mechanical properties (compressive yield strength) at 900 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cr does not result in improved high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance, the hypothesis is falsified

Thus, in this work, four model RHEAs with a variation of Ti, Ta, and V have been designed and produced by mechanical alloying, namely, WVTaTi, WVTaTiCr, WV10Ta10TiCr, and WVTaTi5Cr. This study aims to understand the effects of alloying elements and mechanical alloying on the formation of second phases, microstructure evolution, and mechanical behavior of the WVTaTiCr model alloys. The phase formation of the milled powders and sintered RHEAs was characterized by an X’Pert PRO X-ray diffractometer (XRD, PANalytical, Almelo, The Netherlands) equipped with a copper target. The diffracted intensity of KαCu radiation was measured in the 2θ range from 30° to 110° at a scanning rate of 4° min−1. Microstructure development and chemical analysis of the model RHEAs were examined by a Hitachi-4700 scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi High-Tech Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK). The phase transformation and the crystal structure of different phases were determined using a FEI Tecnai F20 G2 Field Emission Gun TEM (FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR, USA). ImageJ software (V1.53) was used to manually measure the particle size of the model RHEAs. Vickers hardness tests were performed using a load of 9.8 N for a holding time of 15 s at room temperature.

## 3.2.1. WVTaTi Alloys
Figure 2 shows the microstructure development of the WVTaTi model RHEAs after different milling times. For the initial stage of milling (4 h) (see Figure 2a), an inhomogeneous microstructure was obtained. The large dark particle with an irregular shape (see point “A”) has a high content of Ti (49.58 at.%) and O (44.29 at.%), as shown by the corresponding EDS analysis (Table 2), suggesting the formation of titanium oxide. This is a common oxide phase that occurs in the Ti-containing HEAs produced by powder metallurgy routes [,]. It should be noted that, in this study, the dark oxide particles have a similar morphology and contrast, which were difficult to distinguish on the SEM images. Additionally, after 16 h of milling, the microstructure was refined and the repeated cold welding and fracturing of the powder particles promoted the precipitation of (Cr, Ta)-rich phases along with dark oxide particles during a long milling time (see Figure 3c). Furthermore, the BCC matrix phase had a bright contrast (see point “E”) containing a higher amount of W, V, and Ta elements. It is worth noting that the depletion of Ti and Cr in the matrix promoted the formation of Tl-rich oxides and Cr-rich phases in this study.
